title: Multi-Omics Reveals Nonlinear Trajectories and Subtypes in TMJ Disease.
abstract: Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease encompasses a disease continuum from disc displacement to osteoarthritis and perforation, yet patients with similar imaging often follow divergent clinical trajectories. Here, we performed integrated proteomic and metabolomic profiling of synovial fluid from patients across 5 imaging-defined stages (normal disc to advanced degeneration with perforation), quantifying 860 proteins ( n = 91) and 1,027 metabolites ( n = 62). Clinical symptoms did not differ significantly across stages, and unsupervised principal component analysis revealed substantial molecular overlap with no stage separation. Integrated multi-omics analysis revealed that complement activation, cholesterol metabolism, and glutathione-mediated oxidative stress were dynamically associated with disease progression. The imaging severity score (ISS) increased from stage 1 to stage 4 and declined at stage 5, revealing a nonlinear disease pattern. Proteomic and metabolomic modules correlated strongly with ISS ( r = 0.60 and r = -0.49), identifying phospholipid transfer protein (PLTP) and follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL1) as exploratory candidate markers associated with disease severity. Given that anatomical staging failed to capture molecular heterogeneity, exploratory consensus clustering identified 3 molecular phenotypes complementary to anatomical staging: subtype 1 (extracellular matrix remodeling/mechanotransduction), subtype 2 (inflammatory-lipid metabolic), and subtype 3 (immune activated), each with distinct clinical profiles. Together, this study provides the first integrated multi-omics characterization of the TMJ disease continuum, revealing nonlinear progression with disc perforation as a potential transition point and supporting a complementary biology-informed framework for molecular stratification and future mechanism-based therapeutic research.

title: Chronic TFE3 activation in TFE3-associated neurodevelopmental disorder drives metabolic rigidity, lysosomal failure, and cell-extracellular matrix destabilization
abstract: Abstract The transcription factor TFE3 coordinates cellular adaptation to stress. While its acute activation is cytoprotective, chronic TFE3 dysregulation is linked to diverse pathologies. Here, we characterize the cellular landscape of TFE3-NDD, a recently described neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations that disrupt the TFE3-Rag GTPase interface, leading to constitutive TFE3 nuclear localization. Using patient-derived fibroblasts, we show that TFE3-NDD is primarily a metabolic and homeostatic disorder. Mutant cells undergo a profound rewiring toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), resulting in metabolic rigidity and a vulnerability to energy failure. Despite a massive expansion of the lysosomal compartment, we observe a paradoxical qualitative failure characterized by impaired acidification, defective protease maturation, increased lysosomal exocytosis, and aberrant cathepsin K secretion. This secretory phenotype is coupled with a destabilized cell-extracellular matrix interface, marked by impaired migration, defective coordination between actomyosin tension and focal adhesion maturation, and a loss of synaptic stabilizers. Notably, TFE3-NDD shares a signature of high OXPHOS and ferroptosis resistance with TFE3-dependent cancers, such as translocation renal cell carcinoma. Our findings reveal how the chronic hyperactivation of a protective stress-response factor collapses cellular homeostasis, providing a mechanistic framework for the tissue malformations and neurodevelopmental deficits that define TFE3-NDD.

title: Nano-kinetic implant surface mediates osteo-antibacterial synergy through electromagnetic-mechanical coupling
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication of total joint arthroplasty, mainly caused by bacterial biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance. Traditional static surfaces rely on contact killing-based bactericidal properties and cannot reliably clear mature biofilms. In this study, we fabricate a remote-activated dynamic biomimetic system, namely a movable magnetic topographic surface (MMTS). Here we show that under the exposure of external electromagnetic field (EMF), the anchored Janus nano-heterodimers oscillate periodically to mechanically disrupt bacterial membranes and eradicates biofilms of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. This mechanical force can also activates Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), inducing calcium oscillations, upregulating gene expression of Runx2 and BMP2, and enhancing extracellular matrix mineralization. In vivo, MMTS combined with EMF exposure eliminates local infection and promoted osseointegration. This remote-activated dynamic biomimetic strategy offers a promising multifunctional platform for PJI treatment, and improved implant osteointegration in clinical orthopedics.
